text: Ch 1 – Shifting Sands David blinked, clawing his way back up from the relative peace he had been drifting in, Or... he thought he did. It was hard to tell. Everything was dark, dry, and close, the grit scratching faintly against his eyelashes the only real proof his eyes were open at all. He tried to swallow. Instant regret. His throat seized on the attempt, dragged across a thick film of silt and dust that coated his mouth like wet plaster. The cough that followed didn’t come from his chest — it wrung him from the inside out, deep and rolling and loud in the otherwise perfect silence. Pain bloomed through his right shoulder like someone’d lit a flare inside the joint. Not enough to knock him out again — even if for a moment, his body strongly considered it — but enough to burn through the fog at the edge of his thoughts. That arm... where even was it? He shifted, or tried to. The shoulder was wrenched backward at an unnatural angle, trapped somewhere behind him. He couldn’t quite feel it. Not properly. Given the position, it was probably underneath him, and had been for quite some time. How long had he even been out? The air tasted stale. Not rot-stale, just... old . Like it had already been breathed once and politely declined a second use. It clung to the grit in his throat, and for a moment, he couldn’t tell if that was the room’s fault or his own. He tried to roll just enough to shift the pressure off the dead arm. No luck. Something sharp greeted him in every direction — jagged ribs of rubble mixed with the broader flat crush of stone slabs. They pressed in at odd angles, some stabbing through cloth to find skin, others just... there , forcing joints into unnatural postures and denying leverage entirely. The ground beneath him was cool and unmoving, a layer of compacted sand that offered no give and even less comfort. His left arm, at least, was mostly free. Curled near his head, though the space was tight enough he had to move slow just to avoid flaying himself against unseen edges. Fingers crept outward, brushing along the nearby debris. Rough, gritty surfaces met his touch — stone fractured under pressure, shedding streams of dry sand that whispered down onto his face in response. He stilled. Sand? ...Oh. Right. The walkway. The Eyrie. He remembered the brittle stretch of stone underfoot — just wide enough to make him run stupid, just thin enough to make him regret it. Nemesis had swung at him; he remembered that much. A wide, angry arc meant for bone, not structure. It hit a support pillar instead. The whole thing had come down like it was made of plaster and drywall, not ancient stone. He didn’t remember the fall itself — just the sound. The crack of crumbling masonry. A sharp impact. Then darkness. In hindsight, it must’ve taken more than just the walkway. Probably part of the stairwell too. There was way too much debris around him for this to be a single platform collapse. This was an avalanche . Bad maintenance and worse luck, stacked like bricks and now buried in his ribs. Funny thing was... the landing hadn’t even hurt. Not really. He’d hit the ground so hard, there hadn’t been time for pain. Just an impact. Then lights out. Waking up though? That was a different story. His head throbbed, low and deep and constant. Not sharp — just heavy, like the ache had weight. It pressed against the background noise of every other random pain that was gradually waking up and won the argument. Miraculously, his skull had held. No blood in his eyes. No dripping sounds. No open gash. Just a single jagged stone pressed against his temple, insistent and quiet. Not hard enough to break skin. But close. If he’d fallen just slightly to the left... His skull wouldn’t have stopped the blow. It would’ve caved. Like an egg. Hell of a mess, that would've made. Bits of him everywhere. Real inconvenience. He shut that thought down before it went anywhere useful. He swallowed down another cough, forcing it into silence with sheer will. The dust still clawed at the back of his throat, but he wasn’t about to trigger another body-wide shudder. Not with the rubble that had started treating him like a stress ball. Alright. Inventory time. Nothing felt missing . That was a start. His legs were there. Chest still intact, more or less. Bruised? Absolutely. Bleeding? Probably. Slightly crushed in places? Almost definitely. But still whole. The right arm though... He tried to flex the fingers. Nothing. No twitch. No sting. No pull in the tendons. There was just... absence . A hollow space where the arm should’ve existed in his mind. It wasn’t pain that unsettled him — it was the lack of it. That meant the limb had been pinned long enough to kill sensation. Great. That was gonna be a fun reintroduction once the nerves decided to clock back in. He couldn’t even tell if it was broken or just numb. Either way... Problem for later. He shifted his left arm carefully, slow enough to avoid brushing any sharp edges. The motion dragged across stone — rough, uneven — and he curled it inward, trying to map his own torso through the press of rubble. Chest. Side. Hip. Rubble. More rubble. A jagged piece jutting near his ribs. Everything was compact. Tight. Smothered. But not entirely immobile. Each movement sent a faint shiver through the pile. He could feel it above him — stones shifting, not much, but not nothing . Grains of sand trickled down the back of his neck. A whisper of weight. Somewhere near his shoulder, a chunk of debris let out a gritty sigh and resettled. Just a little. The silence around him made it unbearable. It wasn’t dramatic. Nothing
